---
title: "Figure 1.1: Real GDP Growth"
---

![Python: `python/fig-1-1.py`](../images/python/fig-1-1.png)

Four lines of quarterly GDP growth. This is the first and simplest kind of
chart in the REO, so this page explains **every line of the script**. Later
pages only explain what is new.

## The data

`excel_and_png/fig-1-1.xlsx`, sheet `data`, has 10 rows, one per quarter:

| category | USA | CAN | LA7 | CAPDR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024Q1 | 2.93 | 0.99 | 1.87 | 3.65 |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

`category` holds the quarter as text. The other columns are the four series,
named as in the Excel legend. CAPDR has no value in the last quarter.

## The script

### Imports

```python
"""Figure 1.1: Real GDP Growth."""
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.ticker import MultipleLocator

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart
```

The text in triple quotes at the top is the script's *docstring*, its
description. Then come the tools the script uses:

- **numpy** (`np`) is Python's library for arrays of numbers.
- **`MultipleLocator`** puts a tick on the axis at every multiple of a number.
- **From `chart_style`** come the three helpers described in [The shared
  layout](../chart-style.qmd).

### The data and the colours

```python
STEM = "fig-1-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {
    "USA": "#0069A6",
    "CAN": "#444444",
    "LA7": "#682C82",
    "CAPDR": "#C95A0C",
}
```

`STEM` is the chart's name, used both to find the data and to name the
output. `data` is now a pandas DataFrame, the table shown above.

`series_colours` is a *dictionary*: it maps each column name to a colour,
written as a hex code (`#RRGGBB`, the same codes Excel shows under *More
colours*). The colours were read from the published chart. The order of the
entries matters, because it is the order in which the lines are drawn and
listed in the legend.

### The frame

```python
fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Real GDP Growth",
    subtitle="(Year-over-year percent change)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Haver Analytics; IMF, World Economic Outlook database; and\n"
        "IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Aggregates are purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted average.\n"
        "CAPDR = Central America, Panama, and the Dominican Republic; LA7 =\n"
        "Latin America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru,\n"
        "Uruguay)."
    ),
    title_size=13.5,
    left=0.35,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.62,
)
```

`new_chart()` creates the 5 × 5 inch figure, writes the three texts and
returns the figure (`fig`) and the plot area (`ax`).

- **The caption** is a long text written as several pieces in brackets.
  Python joins strings that stand next to each other, so this is one string.
  The `\n` are the line breaks, placed exactly where the published chart has
  them.
- **The space around the plot**, in inches, is set by `left`, `right` and
  `bottom_gap`. Here `bottom_gap=0.62` leaves room for the vertical quarter
  labels. These values were tuned by comparing the result with the published
  chart.

### The lines

```python
# The quarters are categories, plotted at positions 0, 1, 2, ...
x = np.arange(len(data))
for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    # A missing value (CAPDR in the last quarter) leaves a gap in the line.
    values = data[series].astype(float)
    ax.plot(x, values, color=colour, linewidth=1.6,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)
```

The quarters are text, so they are plotted at the positions 0, 1, ..., 9 and
labelled afterwards (see [Categories as
positions](../techniques.qmd#sec-categories)). `len(data)` is the number of
rows.

The `for` loop runs once for each entry of the dictionary. `.items()` gives
the pairs, so in the first round `series` is `"USA"` and `colour` is
`"#0069A6"`. The indented lines are the body of the loop.

- `data[series]` selects one column. `.astype(float)` makes sure it is
  numeric, so that an empty cell becomes `NaN` (*not a number*). matplotlib
  leaves a gap there instead of failing.
- `ax.plot(x, y, ...)` draws one line. `linewidth` is in points.
  `solid_capstyle="round"` rounds the line ends. `label` is the legend text.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", direction="in", length=2, pad=5)

ax.set_ylim(0, 5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(1))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2, pad=6)
```

- **The x-axis.** `set_xticks(positions, labels)` puts a tick and a label at
  each position, and `rotation=90` writes the labels vertically.
  `set_xlim(-0.5, 9.5)` leaves half a step of space at both ends, as Excel
  does for a category axis.
- **The y-axis.** It runs from 0 to 5 with a tick at every whole number. This
  matches the published chart's axis options (minimum 0, maximum 5, major
  unit 1).
- **The ticks.** `tick_params` makes the ticks short (2 points) and point
  into the plot (`direction="in"`). `pad` is the gap between tick and label.
  See [Tick marks and axis lines](../techniques.qmd#sec-ticks).

### The legend and saving

```python
ax.legend(
    loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 0.01), ncol=2,
    handlelength=3.0, columnspacing=2.5, labelspacing=0.15,
)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
```

The legend collects every series drawn with a `label`.

- **Position.** `loc="lower left"` together with `bbox_to_anchor=(0.01,
  0.01)` puts its lower-left corner just inside the lower-left corner of the
  plot.
- **Layout.** `ncol=2` gives two columns. `handlelength` is the length of the
  sample line. The other two arguments are the spacing between columns and
  between rows. See [Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

`save_chart()` writes `python/figures/fig-1-1.png`.

## Try it

A few small changes to get a feel for the code:

- Change `linewidth=1.6` to `2.5` and run the script again.
- Remove `"CAN": "#444444",` from the dictionary: the Canada line and its
  legend entry disappear.
- Change `ncol=2` to `ncol=4` to put the legend on one row.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-1-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-1-1.py"}
"""Figure 1.1: Real GDP Growth."""
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.ticker import MultipleLocator

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart

STEM = "fig-1-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {
    "USA": "#0069A6",
    "CAN": "#444444",
    "LA7": "#682C82",
    "CAPDR": "#C95A0C",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Real GDP Growth",
    subtitle="(Year-over-year percent change)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Haver Analytics; IMF, World Economic Outlook database; and\n"
        "IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Aggregates are purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted average.\n"
        "CAPDR = Central America, Panama, and the Dominican Republic; LA7 =\n"
        "Latin America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru,\n"
        "Uruguay)."
    ),
    title_size=13.5,
    left=0.35,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.62,
)

# The quarters are categories, plotted at positions 0, 1, 2, ...
x = np.arange(len(data))
for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    # A missing value (CAPDR in the last quarter) leaves a gap in the line.
    values = data[series].astype(float)
    ax.plot(x, values, color=colour, linewidth=1.6,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", direction="in", length=2, pad=5)

ax.set_ylim(0, 5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(1))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2, pad=6)

ax.legend(
    loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 0.01), ncol=2,
    handlelength=3.0, columnspacing=2.5, labelspacing=0.15,
)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
